🌎 BEYOND THE 956

LANSING, Mich. — A Lansing convenience store operator has been indicted by a federal grand jury for allegedly turning food assistance benefits into cash at 50 cents on the dollar, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Michigan.

Mohinder Singh, the operator of Romario's convenience store in Lansing — Romario's Party Store in the city's Old Town — was charged by a grand jury with theft or conversion of public money and nine counts of fraud on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the federal program that puts food on the table for low-income families.

The indictment alleges that Singh unlawfully exchanged cash and other ineligible items for SNAP benefits with his customers, and allowed some customers to use SNAP benefits to pay debts they owed him. Singh typically gave SNAP recipients an exchange rate of $0.50 in cash for every $1 of SNAP benefits transferred, according to the indictment. Prosecutors also allege he charged a fee, payable in SNAP benefits, after extending credit to some customers. The government alleges Singh intended more than $1 million in loss.

The Lansing case is one piece of a nationwide enforcement surge announced this week by the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the USDA Office of Inspector General. The coordinated effort brought actions against more than 40 defendants whose alleged or proven schemes caused nearly $45 million in intended losses to the federal government — nearly $42 million of it involving fraud against SNAP benefits.

"These schemes siphoned millions from taxpayers and robbed struggling Americans of the benefits they depend on," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in announcing the surge. U.S. Attorney Timothy VerHey added: "The integrity of the SNAP program is essential to supporting families who rely on it. When individuals or businesses engage in fraud, they deprive vulnerable communities of vital resources."

If convicted of theft or conversion of public money, Singh faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. He faces up to five years in prison on each of the nine SNAP benefits fraud counts. The USDA Office of Inspector General is investigating the case, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Chris O'Connor is prosecuting it.

Why Webb Watch 956 is covering a Michigan case: SNAP serves thousands of families right here in Webb County, and benefit trafficking is one of the fastest ways to drain a program honest families depend on. This federal surge — 40-plus defendants, nearly $42 million — is a reminder that the crackdown on benefit fraud is nationwide, and stores caught buying benefits for cash put every legitimate recipient at risk.

The charges in an indictment are merely accusations, and a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Sources: U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Michigan, U.S. Department of Justice press release, Oct. 21, 2026; WLNS-TV (Lansing), Oct. 21, 2026.

title: Beyond the 956: Lansing store owner indicted in $1 million SNAP fraud scheme, feds say
